SECTION: 3 Large LMs v.s. Small LMs (Pages 2-6)

TOPICS: filter-then-rerank framework, LLM vs SLM performance, few-shot information extraction, experimental setup, prompt engineering, inference speed, task complexity, model limitations

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The proposed filter-then-rerank framework uses SLMs as a filter and LLMs as a reranker (Page 2)
- LLMs have a strong predisposition to false-positive predictions on negative samples, leading to poor performance on easy samples (Page 2)
- The framework yields a consistent F1 improvement averaging 2.4% higher than previous methods (Page 2)
- The research is the first successful attempt to use LLMs to enhance few-shot IE tasks (Page 2)
- The study compares LLMs and SLMs across four IE tasks: Named Entity Recognition (NER), Relation Extraction (RE), Event Detection (ED), and Event Argument Extraction (EAE) (Page 3)
- Experiments are conducted on nine datasets including CONLL03, OntoNotes, FewNERD, TACRED, TACREV, ACE05, MAVEN, and ERE (Page 2)
- The paper evaluates four IE tasks: NER, RE, ED, and EAE (Page 3)
- For EAE, label numbers range from 4 to 168, assessing performance under different schema complexities (Page 3)
- Few-shot datasets are constructed using a K-shot sampling strategy for training and validation sets (Page 3)
- Evaluation uses micro-F1 for NER, RE, and ED, and head-F1 for EAE (Page 3)
- The prompt format consists of three parts: instruction (green), demonstration (blue), and question (black) (Page 3)
- Six LLMs are explored, including OpenAI models like ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0301) (Page 3)
- The main experiments use GPT, CODEX, and Instruct-GPT, with GPT-4 evaluated in Appendix D.3 (Page 4)
- Open-source models include LLaMA-13B and its instruction-tuned version, Vicuna-13B (Page 4)
- Instructions describe the task and enumerate all possible labels, as shown in Figure 1 (Page 4)
- A demo selector $\mathcal{E}$ retrieves a subset of demonstrations based on sentence embedding similarity to the test sample (Page 4)
- Prompt format $f$ uses simple textual templates, such as "Sentence: [S], Entities: ([type1], [entity1]), ([type2], [entity2])..." (Page 4)
- LLMs only outperform SLMs in extremely low-resource settings (Page 5)
- SLMs are generally more effective than LLMs in real-world scenarios due to the practicality of obtaining annotations and the excessive time and budget demands of LLM inference (Page 5)
- LLMs tend to reach a performance plateau with modest increases in sample size, while SLMs show marked enhancement as sample sizes grow (Page 5)
- LLMs perform worse on fine-grained datasets like MAVEN (168 labels) and RAMS (139 labels) compared to CONLL (4 labels) (Page 5)
- Open-source models LLaMA and Vicuna lag behind proprietary LLMs (Page 5)
- Among proprietary LLMs, ChatGPT performs better on NER and EAE but poorer on RE and ED (Page 5)
- LLMs are much slower than SLMs due to more parameters, longer input contexts, and extra response decay (Page 5)
- Prompt sensitivity analysis shows diverse instruction strategies yield comparable results, increasing demo number does not unequivocally enhance performance, and demo selection strategy matters (Page 5)
- LLMs are not good few-shot IE solvers due to underutilized annotations and unexplored task formats (Page 6)
- The filter-then-rerank paradigm uses SLMs as filters and LLMs as rerankers (Page 6)
- LLMs are more familiar with MCQ prompts than IE-format prompts (Zhang et al., 2023a) (Page 6)
- Hard samples are characterized by the need for external knowledge or sophisticated reasoning (Page 6)
- Samples are classified as hard if they have low confidence scores from SLMs (Page 6)

TEXT_EVIDENCE:

- LLMs fail on easy samples due to hallucination and span boundary mismatch (Page 7)
- SLMs outperform LLMs on easy samples because they are better at discerning patterns in negative samples (Page 7)

- Experiments are conducted on FewNERD (NER), TACREV (RE), and ACE05 (ED) datasets (Page 7)
- The method consistently improves performance across three datasets and nine settings, with average F1 gains of 2.4% (without SLM ensemble) and 2.1% (with SLM ensemble) (Page 8)

- The method reduces budget and latency by approximately 80% ~ 90% compared to direct ICL (Page 8)
- GPT-4 generally improves more on hard samples, but InstructGPT surpasses it overall in NER and RE tasks due to its focus on reducing false positives (Page 8)
- The threshold τ to determine sample difficulty is optimized on the valid set (Page 8)
- The paper proposes a "filter-then-rerank" paradigm to leverage SLMs and LLMs (Page 9)
- LLMs are not effective few-shot information extractors in general but significantly improve performance on hard samples when combined with SLMs (Page 9)
- The approach achieves an average 2.4% F1 gain across multiple few-shot IE tasks while minimizing latency and budget costs (Page 9)
- Label filtering reduces demo length and cuts inference costs (Page 9)
- Performance collapses without a filter to identify sample difficulty (Page 9)

SECTION: Abstract (Pages 1-1)

TOPICS: information extraction, large language models, small language models, few-shot learning, in-context learning, model comparison, inference latency, cost efficiency, adaptive filter-then-rerank paradigm

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The paper investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) are effective few-shot solvers for information extraction (IE) tasks compared to fine-tuned Small Language Models (SLMs) (Page 1)
- LLMs are generally not good few-shot extractors due to inferior performance, higher latency, and increased costs (Page 1)
- The study compares LLMs using in-context learning (ICL) with fine-tuned SLMs across nine datasets and four IE tasks (Page 1)
- LLMs only outperform SLMs when annotations are extremely limited (e.g., both label types and samples per label are scarce) (Page 1)
- With more data (hundreds of samples), SLMs significantly outperform LLMs (Page 1)
- LLMs incur greater inference latency and costs than fine-tuned SLMs (Page 1)
- The proposed adaptive filter-then-rerank paradigm uses SLMs as filters and LLMs as rerankers, achieving a 2.4% F1-gain on average (Page 1)
- The paper posits that LLMs are good at hard samples but bad at easy samples (Page 1)

Since most negative samples are easy samples (which could be solved readily by SLMs), the performance of LLMs on easy samples sometimes collapses and are usually much worse than fine-tuned SLMs. Leveraging these findings, we pursue an approach to incorporate LLMs and SLMs within a single system and combine their merits. To this end, we propose a novel filter-then-rerank framework. The basic idea is that SLMs serve as a filter and LLMs as a reranker. Specifically, SLMs initially predict and determine the difficulty of each sample. If the sample is a hard one, we further pass the top- $N$  most-likely candidate labels from SLMs to LLMs for reranking. Otherwise we view the prediction from SLMs as the final decision. By providing easy/hard samples with different solution strategies, our system utilizes each model's strengths to complement each other. Also, it reranks only a small subset of samples and minimizes the extra latency and budgets for calling LLMs. With a modest cost increase, our framework yields a consistent F1 improvement, averaging  $2.4\%$  higher than previous methods on various few-shot IE tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first successful attempt to use LLMs to enhance few-shot IE tasks. 2 Related Work 2.1 LLMs for Information Extraction Recent studies have increasingly explored Information Extraction (IE) tasks using LLMs. Drawing inspiration from instruction tuning (Wei et al., 2022a), several methods (Wadhwa et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a; Lu et al., 2023) transform annotated samples into instruction-answer pairs and then fine-tune LLMs, such as FlanT5 (Chung et al., 2022), on them. Nonetheless, this method necessitates a vast range of samples with diverse schemas and often yields suboptimal results in low-resource scenarios. In the context of few-shot IE tasks, prevalent strategies bifurcate into two main streams. The first approach perceives LLMs as efficient annotators (Ding et al., 2023; Josifoski et al., 2023). It highlights the limitations of LLMs on easy samples and proposes using SLMs as a filter to identify hard samples, which are then reranked by LLMs. The paper reviews related work on LLMs for IE and the inconsistent results in few-shot IE studies, attributing them to a lack of unified benchmarks. The authors conduct comprehensive experiments across four IE tasks and nine datasets with varying schema complexities and low-resource settings.

- The framework yields a consistent F1 improvement averaging 2.4% higher than previous methods.
- The research is the first successful attempt to use LLMs to enhance few-shot IE tasks.
- The study compares LLMs and SLMs across four IE tasks: Named Entity Recognition (NER), Relation Extraction (RE), Event Detection (ED), and one other not fully listed.

Since most negative samples are easy samples (which could be solved readily by SLMs), the performance of LLMs on easy samples sometimes collapses and are usually much worse than fine-tuned SLMs.

Leveraging these findings, we pursue an approach to incorporate LLMs and SLMs within a single system and combine their merits. To this end, we propose a novel filter-then-rerank framework. The basic idea is that SLMs serve as a filter and LLMs as a reranker. Specifically, SLMs initially predict and determine the difficulty of each sample. If the sample is a hard one, we further pass the top- $N$  most-likely candidate labels from SLMs to LLMs for reranking. Otherwise we view the prediction from SLMs as the final decision. By providing easy/hard samples with different solution strategies, our system utilizes each model's strengths to complement each other. Also, it reranks only a small subset of samples and minimizes the extra latency and budgets for calling LLMs. With a modest cost increase, our framework yields a consistent F1 improvement, averaging  $2.4\%$  higher than previous methods on various few-shot IE tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first successful attempt to use LLMs to enhance few-shot IE tasks.
2 Related Work
2.1 LLMs for Information Extraction

Recent studies have increasingly explored Information Extraction (IE) tasks using LLMs. Drawing inspiration from instruction tuning (Wei et al., 2022a), several methods (Wadhwa et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a; Lu et al., 2023) transform annotated samples into instruction-answer pairs and then fine-tune LLMs, such as FlanT5 (Chung et al., 2022), on them. Nonetheless, this method necessitates a vast range of samples with diverse schemas and often yields suboptimal results in low-resource scenarios. In the context of few-shot IE tasks, prevalent strategies bifurcate into two main streams. The first approach perceives LLMs as efficient annotators (Ding et al., 2023; Josifoski et al., 2023). In these methods, they produce a plethora of pseudolabeled samples through LLMs and leverage the enhanced annotations to train SLMs. Conversely, the latter approach employs LLMs in inference using the ICL paradigm, which is the focus of our subsequent discussion.
2.2 Few-shot IE with ICL

Regarding few-shot IE tasks, recent studies intensively compare the performance between SLMs and LLMs but yield inconsistent conclusions. Some studies favor LLMs as competent few-shot extractors (Agrawal et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023b; Li et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023a; Wadhwa et al., 2023), while others dispute this claim (Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2023). This discrepancy leaves the question of whether LLMs perform competitively on few-shot IE tasks unresolved, thus hindering the advances of this domain.

We attribute such disagreement to the absence of an comprehensive and unified benchmark. Existing studies usually vary in tasks, datasets, and few-shot settings. Furthermore, some studies rely on overly simplistic datasets (Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023) and may exaggerate the effectiveness of LLMs. Driven by these findings, our research undertakes comprehensive experiments across four IE tasks, nine datasets with various schema complexities (from coarse-grained to fine-grained) and low-resource settings.

In addition to the empirical study, we develop an innovative filter-then-rerank paradigm to combine the strengths of both LLMs and SLMs. It utilizes prompting strategies akin to QA4RE (Zhang et al., 2023a), transforming IE tasks into multi-choice questions. However, our method stands apart by integrating SLMs and LLMs within a single framework. This incorporation (1) enables our paradigm applicable to various IE tasks by providing candidate spans in the text and (2) achieves promising performance under low-resource IE scenarios.

3.4 Main Results We summarize the main experimental outcomes in Figure 2, indicating that LLMs only outperform SLMs in environments with restricted labels and samples. Conversely, SLMs are generally more effective. Given (1) the practicality of fine-grained IE tasks and the manageable effort of obtaining 10-20 annotations per label and (2) the excessive time and budget demands of LLM inference, we conclude that LLMs are not as effective as supervised SLMs for few-shot IE tasks under real scenarios. We detail our findings as below. Performance w.r.t sample number. The performance dynamics of SLMs and LLMs are influenced by variations in sample size. Under extremely low-resource (1-shot or 5-shot) settings, LLMs sometimes present superior performance than SLMs. Yet, LLMs tend to reach a performance plateau with only modest increases in sample size. Conversely, SLMs demonstrate marked performance enhancement as sample sizes grow. This trend is evident in Figure 2, where the SLM trajectories (represented by dashed lines) ascend more steeply compared to the LLM ones (solid lines). Performance w.r.t label number. Compared with SLMs, LLMs tend to struggle on fine-grained datasets. For instance, LLMs perform relatively worse on MAVEN and RAMS datasets (with 168/139 labels) than on CONLL (4 labels only). Detailed quantitative results are shown in Appendix E.1, illustrating a clear negative correlation between the label number and the result disparity between LLMs and SLMs across various IE tasks. Comparisons among LLMs. We observe performance variability among LLMs. (1) Open-source models, LLaMA and Vicuna, significantly lag behind proprietary LLMs across all few-shot IE tasks. (2) Among proprietary LLMs, ChatGPT performs better on NER and EAE tasks, but poorer so on RE and ED tasks. InstructGPT and CODEX demonstrate comparable performance across these tasks. LLMs show limited inference speed. We compare the inference speed of different methods and show their results in Table 1. We observe that LLMs is much slower than SLMs since they have much more parameters, longer input contexts and extra response decay (if external APIs applied). 3.5 Analysis on Prompt Sensitivity Previous work (Lu et al., 2022b) indicates that the efficacy of LLMs on specific tasks can be significantly influenced by the construction of the prompt. We leave comprehensive details of the variants and their results to Appendix E.2-E.5, and illustrate salient findings in Figure 3. The text concludes that SLMs are generally more effective than LLMs in real-world scenarios due to the practicality of obtaining annotations and the excessive time and budget demands of LLM inference. Key findings include that LLMs only outperform SLMs in extremely low-resource settings, struggle with fine-grained datasets, and exhibit significant inference speed limitations. The page includes a detailed analysis of prompt sensitivity, supported by Figure 3, which shows that instruction format has minimal impact, increasing demonstration samples does not always help, and the selection strategy of demonstrations is crucial. Table 1 quantifies the inference speed, showing LLMs like LLaMA are orders of magnitude slower than SLMs.

**Text Evidence:**
- LLMs only outperform SLMs in environments with restricted labels and samples.
- SLMs are generally more effective for few-shot IE tasks under real scenarios.
- LLMs tend to reach a performance plateau with modest increases in sample size, while SLMs show marked enhancement as sample sizes grow.
- LLMs perform worse on fine-grained datasets like MAVEN (168 labels) and RAMS (139 labels) compared to CONLL (4 labels).
- Open-source models LLaMA and Vicuna lag behind proprietary LLMs.
- Among proprietary LLMs, ChatGPT performs better on NER and EAE but poorer on RE and ED.
- LLMs are much slower than SLMs due to more parameters, longer input contexts, and extra response decay.

elements.text: 3.4 Main Results

We summarize the main experimental outcomes in Figure 2, indicating that LLMs only outperform SLMs in environments with restricted labels and samples. Conversely, SLMs are generally more effective. Given (1) the practicality of fine-grained IE tasks and the manageable effort of obtaining 10-20 annotations per label and (2) the excessive time and budget demands of LLM inference, we conclude that LLMs are not as effective as supervised SLMs for few-shot IE tasks under real scenarios. We detail our findings as below.

Performance w.r.t sample number. The performance dynamics of SLMs and LLMs are influenced by variations in sample size. Under extremely low-resource (1-shot or 5-shot) settings, LLMs sometimes present superior performance than SLMs. Yet, LLMs tend to reach a performance plateau with only modest increases in sample size. Conversely, SLMs demonstrate marked performance enhancement as sample sizes grow. This trend is evident in Figure 2, where the SLM trajectories (represented by dashed lines) ascend more steeply compared to the LLM ones (solid lines).

Performance w.r.t label number. Compared with SLMs, LLMs tend to struggle on fine-grained datasets. For instance, LLMs perform relatively worse on MAVEN and RAMS datasets (with 168/139 labels) than on CONLL (4 labels only). Detailed quantitative results are shown in Appendix E.1, illustrating a clear negative correlation between the label number and the result disparity between LLMs and SLMs across various IE tasks.
Comparisons among LLMs. We observe performance variability among LLMs. (1) Open-source models, LLaMA and Vicuna, significantly lag behind proprietary LLMs across all few-shot IE tasks.
(2) Among proprietary LLMs, ChatGPT performs better on NER and EAE tasks, but poorer so on RE and ED tasks. InstructGPT and CODEX demonstrate comparable performance across these tasks.

LLMs show limited inference speed. We compare the inference speed of different methods and show their results in Table 1. We observe that LLMs is much slower than SLMs since they have much more parameters, longer input contexts and extra response decay (if external APIs applied).
3.5 Analysis on Prompt Sensitivity

Previous work (Lu et al., 2022b) indicates that the efficacy of LLMs on specific tasks can be significantly influenced by the construction of the prompt. To ensure that LLMs' suboptimal outcomes are not erroneously ascribed to inappropriate prompt designs, we meticulously examine the impact of diverse prompt variations from four aspects, i.e., instruction format, demo number, demo selector and prompt format. We leave comprehensive details of the variants and their results to Appendix E.2-E.5, and illustrate salient findings in Figure 3. Our findings include that (1) diverse instruction strategies yield comparable results in IE task; (2) increasing the number of samples in demonstrations does not unequivocally enhance performance; and (3) The selection strategy of demonstration matters, and retrieval based on sentence embedding

Underutilized Annotations. We notice that LLMs appear to benefit less from additional annotations, i.e., more training samples and label types, than SLMs. We speculate that LLMs are constrained by ICL in two ways. (1) More samples: The number of effective samples for LLMs, those in demos, is limited by maximum input length. Moreover, we also observe LLMs' performance plateaus in some tasks before reaching this limit (see Appendix E.3). Meanwhile, SLMs can continually learn from more samples through supervised learning, widening the performance gap as annotated samples increase. (2) More labels: LLMs struggle with fine-grained datasets. It suggests a difficulty in understanding numerous labels and their subtle interactions merely from the given instruction and exemplars for LLMs. Also, the examples per label in demos decrease as label types increase. Unexplored Task format. As stated in Zhang et al. (2023a), IE-related tasks are scarce in the widely-used instruction tuning datasets like Wei et al. (2022a) and Wang et al. (2022). Furthermore, the highly-flexible format of NER and ED tasks impair the ICL abilities<sup>7</sup>. (b)The New Yorker is a broadcast program. (c)The New Yorker is a kind of written art. (d)The New Yorker is a media/newspaper organization. Analysis: The New Yorker is a well-known American magazine that has been published since 1925, and is primarily known for its long-form journalism, commentary, and satire. It has a reputation for publishing high-quality writing on a wide variety of topics, including politics, culture, and the arts. So The New Yorker is a media/newspaper organization. Correct Answer: (d) Figure 4: Multi-choice question (MCQ) prompt. To mitigate LLMs' drawbacks mentioned above, we propose a filter-then-rerank paradigm to integrate both SLMs and LLMs within the same system. This paradigm uses SLMs as filters to select the top- $N$  candidate labels, then LLMs rerank them to make final decisions. By using SLM-generated candidate answers, the focus of LLMs shifts from sentence-level (i.e., identifying all entities/events in the sentence) to sample-level (i.e., determining single entity/event candidate provided). Each question now corresponds to a single sample, allowing us to reframe prompts as multi-choice questions (MCQ; shown in Figure 4) problem. Under such format, each candidate label is converted to a choice by pre-defined templates. We claim filter-then-rerank paradigm is more likely to elicit the powers of LLMs and smoothly solve few-shot IE tasks because: (1) LLMs are more familiar with MCQ prompts than IE-format prompts (Zhang et al., 2023a). We hypothesize that LLMs are more proficient than SLMs on hard samples. These samples are characterized by their requisite for external knowledge acquisition or sophisticated reasoning strategies, areas where LLMs can leverage their extensive parametric knowledge bases and inherent reasoning mechanisms. In contrast, SLMs often falter with such samples, constrained by their restricted modeling capacities. We leverage an unsupervised metric from SLMs to evaluate the difficulty of samples. This page presents experimental results and analysis on the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) compared to Supervised Small Models (SLMs) in information extraction tasks. The core finding, illustrated in Figure 5, is that LLMs excel at handling hard samples (low confidence scores) but underperform on easy samples (high confidence scores), leading to a significant degradation in overall performance when used for reranking. This is attributed to LLMs' tendency for false-positive predictions on negative samples, as quantified in Table 2, which shows a much higher ratio of negative to positive samples for easy instances. Based on these findings, the paper proposes an "adaptive filter-then-rerank" paradigm (Section 5) that uses SLMs as a cost-efficient filter and LLMs only for reranking difficult cases.

- Experiments are conducted on FewNERD (NER), TACREV (RE), and ACE05 (ED) datasets.

pages.summary:
This page presents a comprehensive analysis of an adaptive filter-then-rerank paradigm for language model tasks. It details the method's architecture, which uses a small language model (SLM) as a filter to identify hard samples, which are then reranked by a large language model (LLM). The page includes Figure 6, which visually outlines this process, and references Table 3 and Table 4 for performance results. Key findings show that the method achieves significant F1 gains (2.4% and 2.1%) with InstructGPT and GPT-4, respectively, while drastically reducing computational cost by 80-90% compared to direct in-context learning. The analysis highlights that only a small fraction (0.5%-10%) of samples are hard, but reranking them yields substantial performance boosts (10%-25% absolute F1 gains), demonstrating the efficiency of the approach.

**Text Evidence:**
- The method consistently improves performance across three datasets and nine settings, with average F1 gains of 2.4% (without SLM ensemble) and 2.1% (with SLM ensemble).
- Only a minor fraction (0.5% ~ 10%) of samples are deemed hard and reranked, yet this results in a substantial performance boost (10% ~ 25% absolute F1 gains).
- The method reduces budget and latency by approximately 80% ~ 90% compared to direct ICL.
- GPT-4 generally improves more on hard samples, but InstructGPT surpasses it overall in NER and RE tasks due to its focus on reducing false positives.
- The threshold τ to determine sample difficulty is optimized on the valid set.

**Visual Evidence:**
<figure_summary>Figure 6: The overall architecture of our adaptive filter-then-rerank paradigm. We color easy samples in orange and hard samples in pink. For easy samples, the final predictions are exactly from the SLM-based methods. For hard samples, the top-N predictions from SLMs are fed into LLMs as the format of multiple-choice questions (pink box). The question is paired with demos (green box). LLMs rerank these N candidates and generate the final prediction.</figure_summary>

(3) LF (label filtering): We retain all labels as candidate choices for reranking, instead of only the top- $N$  labels from the SLMs. (4) AD (adaptive): We feed all samples, not just hard ones, to the LLMs. We show their results in Table 5 and see that (1) Demos with explanations consistently enhance the reranking ability of LLMs across all datasets. (2) Demos without explanations also contribute to performance improvement. (3) Label filtering results in gains and notably reduces the demo length, hence cutting inference costs. (4) The performance collapses without a filter to identify sample difficulty, reiterating the need for an integrated SLM-LLM system to complement each other. 6 Conclusion Through an extensive empirical study on nine datasets spanning four IE tasks, we find that LLMs, despite their superiority in extreme low-resource scenarios, are not effective few-shot information extractors in general. They struggle with IE-related prompts, have limited demonstration capacity, and incur high inference costs. However, LLMs significantly improve the performance on hard samples when combined with SLM. Building on these insights, we propose an adaptive filter-then-erank paradigm to leverage the strengths of SLMs and LLMs and mitigate their limitations. This approach consistently achieves promising results, with an average  $2.4\%$  F1 gain across multiple few-shot IE tasks, while minimizing latency and budget costs.

This page presents a comprehensive evaluation of information extraction methods, focusing on the proposed filter-then-rerank paradigm that combines small language models (SLMs) and large language models (LLMs). It includes three tables: Table 3 compares the overall performance of various ICL and supervised methods across nine datasets; Table 4 quantifies the F1-score improvements from reranking; and Table 5 details an ablation study showing the impact of key components like CoT, demos, label filtering, and adaptive sampling. The page also features Figure 7, a bar chart illustrating the financial and time costs of different approaches, and concludes with a summary of findings, highlighting a 2.4% average F1 gain and significant cost reductions.

**Text Evidence:**
- The paper proposes a "filter-then-rerank" paradigm to leverage SLMs and LLMs.
- LLMs are not effective few-shot information extractors in general but significantly improve performance on hard samples when combined with SLMs.
- The approach achieves an average 2.4% F1 gain across multiple few-shot IE tasks while minimizing latency and budget costs.
- Label filtering reduces demo length and cuts inference costs.
- Performance collapses without a filter to identify sample difficulty.

Through an extensive empirical study on nine datasets spanning four IE tasks, we find that LLMs, despite their superiority in extreme low-resource scenarios, are not effective few-shot information extractors in general. They struggle with IE-related prompts, have limited demonstration capacity, and incur high inference costs. However, LLMs significantly improve the performance on hard samples when combined with SLM. This page presents a comprehensive evaluation of information extraction methods, focusing on the proposed filter-then-rerank paradigm that combines small language models (SLMs) and large language models (LLMs). It includes three tables: Table 3 compares the overall performance of various ICL and supervised methods across nine datasets; Table 4 quantifies the F1-score improvements from reranking; and Table 5 details an ablation study showing the impact of key components like CoT, demos, label filtering, and adaptive sampling. The page also features Figure 7, a bar chart illustrating the financial and time costs of different approaches, and concludes with a summary of findings, highlighting a 2.4% average F1 gain and significant cost reductions.

**Text Evidence:**
- The paper proposes a "filter-then-rerank" paradigm to leverage SLMs and LLMs.
- LLMs are not effective few-shot information extractors in general but significantly improve performance on hard samples when combined with SLMs.
- The approach achieves an average 2.4% F1 gain across multiple few-shot IE tasks while minimizing latency and budget costs.
- Label filtering reduces demo length and cuts inference costs.
- Performance collapses without a filter to identify sample difficulty.

pages.ocr_text: Limitations We do work hard to find better prompts to elicit the power of LLMs on few-shot IE tasks in Section 3.5, by exploring various kinds of LLMs, demonstration strategies and prompt formats. We find that different prompt variants do not significantly impact in-context learning abilities. As an empirical study, we acknowledge the potential existence of a lottery prompt superior to our explored prompts. However, it seems unlikely that an improved prompt would substantially alter our conclusions. Another common risk when evaluating LLMs on public benchmark is their potential memorization of samples tested. To mitigate such potential contamination, we use earlier and stable versions of these models rather than the newer and updated ones (for example, gpt-4-0314 instead of gpt-4). Even if such contamination makes abilities of LLMs overestimated, our primary conclusions remain unchanged because we find that LLMs are NOT good few-shot information extractors. Regarding our adaptive filter-then-erank paradigm, a key limitation lies in how to assess sample difficulty. In this work, we employ a simple unsupervised metric, i.e., the maximum probabilities from SLMs. This is predicated on the assumption that SLMs are well-calibrated (Guo et al., 2017). However, it is an obviously imperfect assumption. We envision that calibrating SLMs-based filters or developing an advanced difficulty metric could substantially enhance LLM rerankers' performance. We leave them for future work. This page contains the Limitations, Acknowledgement, and References sections of a research paper. The Limitations section discusses potential issues with prompt engineering for LLMs in few-shot information extraction tasks, noting that different prompt variants do not significantly impact performance and that model memorization on public benchmarks is a concern mitigated by using older model versions like gpt-4-0314. It also identifies a key limitation in the adaptive filter-then-rerank paradigm: the use of a simple unsupervised metric (maximum probabilities from SLMs) to assess sample difficulty, which relies on the imperfect assumption that SLMs are well-calibrated. The Acknowledgement section details funding sources including the RIE2020 Industry Alignment Fund, Singapore MOE AcRF Tier 1 grant, and industry partner contributions. The References section lists numerous academic papers related to large language models, information extraction, and machine learning.

**Text Evidence:**
- The study explores various LLMs, demonstration strategies, and prompt formats in Section 3.5.
- Different prompt variants do not significantly impact in-context learning abilities.
- The primary conclusion that LLMs are NOT good few-shot information extractors remains unchanged despite potential model memorization.
- An improved prompt is unlikely to substantially alter the conclusions.
- To mitigate contamination, earlier and stable versions of models are used (e.g., gpt-4-0314 instead of gpt-4).
- A key limitation is assessing sample difficulty using a simple unsupervised metric based on maximum probabilities from SLMs.
- This metric assumes SLMs are well-calibrated, an imperfect assumption.
- Calibrating SLMs-based filters or developing an advanced difficulty metric could enhance performance.
- The study is supported by the RIE2020 IAF-ICP Funding Initiative, Singapore MOE AcRF Tier 1 grant, and industry partners.

We do work hard to find better prompts to elicit the power of LLMs on few-shot IE tasks in Section 3.5, by exploring various kinds of LLMs, demonstration strategies and prompt formats. We find that different prompt variants do not significantly impact in-context learning abilities. As an empirical study, we acknowledge the potential existence of a lottery prompt superior to our explored prompts. Another common risk when evaluating LLMs on public benchmark is their potential memorization of samples tested. To mitigate such potential contamination, we use earlier and stable versions of these models rather than the newer and updated ones (for example, gpt-4-0314 instead of gpt-4). Even if such contamination makes abilities of LLMs overestimated, our primary conclusions remain unchanged because we find that LLMs are NOT good few-shot information extractors.

Regarding our adaptive filter-then-erank paradigm, a key limitation lies in how to assess sample difficulty. In this work, we employ a simple unsupervised metric, i.e., the maximum probabilities from SLMs. This is predicated on the assumption that SLMs are well-calibrated (Guo et al., 2017). We find that different prompt variants do not significantly impact in-context learning abilities. As an empirical study, we acknowledge the potential existence of a lottery prompt superior to our explored prompts. However, it seems unlikely that an improved prompt would substantially alter our conclusions. Another common risk when evaluating LLMs on public benchmark is their potential memorization of samples tested. To mitigate such potential contamination, we use earlier and stable versions of these models rather than the newer and updated ones (for example, gpt-4-0314 instead of gpt-4). Even if such contamination makes abilities of LLMs overestimated, our primary conclusions remain unchanged because we find that LLMs are NOT good few-shot information extractors. Regarding our adaptive filter-then-erank paradigm, a key limitation lies in how to assess sample difficulty. In this work, we employ a simple unsupervised metric, i.e., the maximum probabilities from SLMs. This is predicated on the assumption that SLMs are well-calibrated (Guo et al., 2017). However, it is an obviously imperfect assumption. We envision that calibrating SLMs-based filters or developing an advanced difficulty metric could substantially enhance LLM rerankers' performance. This page contains the Limitations, Acknowledgement, and References sections of a research paper. The Limitations section discusses potential issues with prompt engineering for LLMs in few-shot information extraction tasks, noting that different prompt variants do not significantly impact performance and that model memorization on public benchmarks is a concern mitigated by using older model versions like gpt-4-0314. It also identifies a key limitation in the adaptive filter-then-rerank paradigm: the use of a simple unsupervised metric (maximum probabilities from SLMs) to assess sample difficulty, which relies on the imperfect assumption that SLMs are well-calibrated. The Acknowledgement section details funding sources including the RIE2020 Industry Alignment Fund, Singapore MOE AcRF Tier 1 grant, and industry partner contributions. The References section lists numerous academic papers related to large language models, information extraction, and machine learning.

**Text Evidence:**

- Different prompt variants do not significantly impact in-context learning abilities.
- The primary conclusion that LLMs are NOT good few-shot information extractors remains unchanged despite potential model memorization.
- An improved prompt is unlikely to substantially alter the conclusions.
- To mitigate contamination, earlier and stable versions of models are used (e.g., gpt-4-0314 instead of gpt-4).
- A key limitation is assessing sample difficulty using a simple unsupervised metric based on maximum probabilities from SLMs.
- This metric assumes SLMs are well-calibrated, an imperfect assumption.

elements.text: Limitations

We do work hard to find better prompts to elicit the power of LLMs on few-shot IE tasks in Section 3.5, by exploring various kinds of LLMs, demonstration strategies and prompt formats. We find that different prompt variants do not significantly impact in-context learning abilities. As an empirical study, we acknowledge the potential existence of a lottery prompt superior to our explored prompts. However, it seems unlikely that an improved prompt would substantially alter our conclusions.

Another common risk when evaluating LLMs on public benchmark is their potential memorization of samples tested. To mitigate such potential contamination, we use earlier and stable versions of these models rather than the newer and updated ones (for example, gpt-4-0314 instead of gpt-4). Even if such contamination makes abilities of LLMs overestimated, our primary conclusions remain unchanged because we find that LLMs are NOT good few-shot information extractors.

Regarding our adaptive filter-then-erank paradigm, a key limitation lies in how to assess sample difficulty. In this work, we employ a simple unsupervised metric, i.e., the maximum probabilities from SLMs. This is predicated on the assumption that SLMs are well-calibrated (Guo et al., 2017). However, it is an obviously imperfect assumption. We envision that calibrating SLMs-based filters or developing an advanced difficulty metric could substantially enhance LLM rerankers' performance. We leave them for future work.

pages.ocr_text: Limitations We do work hard to find better prompts to elicit the power of LLMs on few-shot IE tasks in Section 3.5, by exploring various kinds of LLMs, demonstration strategies and prompt formats. We find that different prompt variants do not significantly impact in-context learning abilities. As an empirical study, we acknowledge the potential existence of a lottery prompt superior to our explored prompts. However, it seems unlikely that an improved prompt would substantially alter our conclusions. Another common risk when evaluating LLMs on public benchmark is their potential memorization of samples tested. To mitigate such potential contamination, we use earlier and stable versions of these models rather than the newer and updated ones (for example, gpt-4-0314 instead of gpt-4). Even if such contamination makes abilities of LLMs overestimated, our primary conclusions remain unchanged because we find that LLMs are NOT good few-shot information extractors. Regarding our adaptive filter-then-erank paradigm, a key limitation lies in how to assess sample difficulty. In this work, we employ a simple unsupervised metric, i.e., the maximum probabilities from SLMs. This is predicated on the assumption that SLMs are well-calibrated (Guo et al., 2017). However, it is an obviously imperfect assumption. We envision that calibrating SLMs-based filters or developing an advanced difficulty metric could substantially enhance LLM rerankers' performance. We leave them for future work. This page contains the Limitations, Acknowledgement, and References sections of a research paper. The Limitations section discusses potential issues with prompt engineering for LLMs in few-shot information extraction tasks, noting that different prompt variants do not significantly impact performance and that model memorization on public benchmarks is a concern mitigated by using older model versions like gpt-4-0314. It also identifies a key limitation in the adaptive filter-then-rerank paradigm: the use of a simple unsupervised metric (maximum probabilities from SLMs) to assess sample difficulty, which relies on the imperfect assumption that SLMs are well-calibrated. The Acknowledgement section details funding sources including the RIE2020 Industry Alignment Fund, Singapore MOE AcRF Tier 1 grant, and industry partner contributions. The References section lists numerous academic papers related to large language models, information extraction, and machine learning.

elements.text: Limitations

We do work hard to find better prompts to elicit the power of LLMs on few-shot IE tasks in Section 3.5, by exploring various kinds of LLMs, demonstration strategies and prompt formats. We find that different prompt variants do not significantly impact in-context learning abilities. As an empirical study, we acknowledge the potential existence of a lottery prompt superior to our explored prompts. However, it seems unlikely that an improved prompt would substantially alter our conclusions.

Another common risk when evaluating LLMs on public benchmark is their potential memorization of samples tested. To mitigate such potential contamination, we use earlier and stable versions of these models rather than the newer and updated ones (for example, gpt-4-0314 instead of gpt-4). Even if such contamination makes abilities of LLMs overestimated, our primary conclusions remain unchanged because we find that LLMs are NOT good few-shot information extractors.

Regarding our adaptive filter-then-erank paradigm, a key limitation lies in how to assess sample difficulty. In this work, we employ a simple unsupervised metric, i.e., the maximum probabilities from SLMs. This is predicated on the assumption that SLMs are well-calibrated (Guo et al., 2017). However, it is an obviously imperfect assumption. We envision that calibrating SLMs-based filters or developing an advanced difficulty metric could substantially enhance LLM rerankers' performance. We leave them for future work.

- For NER and ED tasks, a greedy sampling algorithm (Algorithm 1) is used because exact sampling is NP-complete.
- The ratio of positive to negative sentences is maintained at 1:1.
- Five supervised methods (Fine-tuning, FSLs, KnowPrompt, PAIE, UIE) are adopted to evaluate SLMs.

We construct few-shot IE datasets and conduct the empirical study on nine datasets spanning four tasks, with varying schema complexities ranging from 4 to 168. We show their statistics in Table 6.
A.2 Details of Few-shot IE Datasets
Sampling Algorithm for Train/Valid Datasets.

We downsample sentences from original training dataset to construct few-shot training and valid datasets. We adopt  $K$ -shot sampling strategy that each label has (at least)  $K$  samples. We set  $6K$ -values (1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100) for RE tasks and 4  $K$ -values (1, 5, 10, 20) for other tasks. For RE task, each sentence has exactly one relation and we simply select  $K$  sentences for each label. For NER, ED and EAE tasks, each sentence is possible to contain more than one entities/events/arguments. Since our sampling is at sentence-level, the algorithm of accurate sampling, i.e., finding exactly  $K$  samples for each label, is NP-complete<sup>8</sup> and unlikely to find a practical solution. Therefore we follow Yang and Katiyar (2020) adopting a greedy sampling algorithm to select sentences for NER and ED tasks, as shown in Algorithm 1. Note that the actual sample number of each label can be larger than  $K$  under this sampling strategy. For all three tasks, we additionally sample negative sentences (without any defined labels) and make the ratio of positive sentences (with at least one label) and negative sentences as 1:1. The statistics of the curated datasets are listed in Table 7.
Algorithm 1 Greedy Sampling

Based on the subsets constructed above, we optionally further split them into training and valid sets. For few-shot datasets with more than 300 sentences, we additionally split  $10\%$  sentences as the valid set and the remaining sentences as training set. This page details the construction of few-shot information extraction (IE) datasets for empirical study, focusing on nine datasets across four tasks with schema complexities from 4 to 168. It describes a K-shot sampling strategy and introduces Algorithm 1, a greedy sampling method for NER and ED tasks due to the NP-completeness of exact sampling. The section also outlines five supervised methods (Fine-tuning, FSLs, KnowPrompt, PAIE, UIE) used to evaluate large language models on these tasks.

**Text Evidence:**
- Nine datasets spanning four tasks with schema complexities from 4 to 168 are used.
- A K-shot sampling strategy is employed, with K-values of (1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100) for RE tasks and (1, 5, 10, 20) for other tasks.
- For NER and ED tasks, a greedy sampling algorithm (Algorithm 1) is used because exact sampling is NP-complete.
- The ratio of positive to negative sentences is maintained at 1:1.
- Five supervised methods (Fine-tuning, FSLs, KnowPrompt, PAIE, UIE) are adopted to evaluate SLMs.

It includes two tables: Table 6 provides comprehensive statistics for nine datasets across various tasks, including the number of labels, sentences, and mentions for training and test sets. Table 7 details the statistics of few-shot training sets, showing average numbers of labels, sentences, samples, and shots for different settings (1-shot to 100-shot) across multiple datasets. **Text Evidence:**
- The paper uses RoBERTa-large as a backbone for KnowPrompt and other methods.
- Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) training is adopted to save memory.

- For KnowPrompt, 10 epochs are set for 50- and 100-shot datasets, and 50 epochs for others.
- PAIE uses BART-large and has specific hyperparameters for the ERE dataset (1000 steps, batch size 16, learning rate 2e-5).
- UIE uses T5-large with a batch size of 4, 4000 training steps, and a maximum input length of 800.

- Page 15: The paper uses RoBERTa-large as a backbone for KnowPrompt and other methods. Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) training is adopted to save memory. Experiments are run on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU for most methods, except UIE which uses a Quadro RTX8000 GPU. For KnowPrompt, 10 epochs are set for 50- and 100-shot datasets, and 50 epochs for others. PAIE uses BART-large and has specific hyperparameters for the ERE dataset (1000 steps, batch size 16, learning rate 2e-5). UIE uses T5-large with a batch size of 4, 4000 training steps, and a maximum input length of 800. The empirical study explores the ICL abilities of five LLMs from two sources, primarily OpenAI.
- Page 16: Experiments use OpenAI models (CODEX, InstructGPT, ChatGPT) via APIs and open-source models (LLaMA-13B, Vicuna-13B) without fine-tuning. For all main experiments, the sampling temperature is set to 0 (greedy decoding). Table 8 shows that setting t=0 yields significantly higher F1-scores than t=0.7 for all three datasets (FewNERD, TACREV, ACE05). Table 9 demonstrates that Auto-CoT drastically reduces performance, with F1-score drops of 17.4 points on FewNERD, 35.3 points on TACREV, and 4.6 points on ACE05. The authors speculate the degradation is due to increased sample length, label discrepancy, and low-quality generated rationales.

This page presents detailed experimental setup information and dataset statistics for a study on few-shot information extraction. It includes two tables: Table 6 provides comprehensive statistics for nine datasets across various tasks, including the number of labels, sentences, and mentions for training and test sets. Table 7 details the statistics of few-shot training sets, showing average numbers of labels, sentences, samples, and shots for different settings (1-shot to 100-shot) across multiple datasets. The text describes the implementation details for several methods (KnowPrompt, PAIE, UIE, LLMs), specifying their backbone models, hyperparameters, and hardware used, such as RoBERTa-large, BART-large, T5-large, and NVIDIA GPUs.

**Text Evidence:**
- The paper uses RoBERTa-large as a backbone for KnowPrompt and other methods.
- Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) training is adopted to save memory.
- Experiments are run on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU for most methods, except UIE which uses a Quadro RTX8000 GPU.
- For KnowPrompt, 10 epochs are set for 50- and 100-shot datasets, and 50 epochs for others.
- PAIE uses BART-large and has specific hyperparameters for the ERE dataset (1000 steps, batch size 16, learning rate 2e-5).
- UIE uses T5-large with a batch size of 4, 4000 training steps, and a maximum input length of 800.
- The empirical study explores the ICL abilities of five LLMs from two sources, primarily OpenAI.

KnowPrompt We implement this method based on original source code<sup>10</sup>, and use RoBERTa-large as our backbones. We set 10 maximum epochs for 50- and 100-shot datasets, and as 50 epochs for other datasets. We keep all other hyperparameters as default, and run each experiment on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU.

PAIE We implement this method on original source code<sup>11</sup>, and use BART-large (Lewis et al., 2020) as backbones. We keep all hyperparameters as default for ACE and RAMS dataset. For ERE dataset, we set the training step as 1000, the batch size as 16 and the learning rate as 2e-5. We run each experiment on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. UIE We implement this method based on original source code<sup>12</sup>, and use T5-large (Raffel et al., 2020) as the backbones. We run each experiment on a single NVIDIA Quadro RTX8000 GPU. We set the batch size as 4 with 4000 training steps. We set the maximum input length as 800 and the learning rate as 1e-4.

Regarding our empirical study, we explore the ICL abilities of LLMs on few-shot IE tasks. We mainly use five LLMs from two sources. (1) OpenAI

models: CODEX (code-davinci-002; Chen et al. 2021), InstructGPT (text-davinci-003; Ouyang et al. 2022), and ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0301). (2) Open-source models: LLaMA-13B (Touvron et al., 2023) and its instruction-tuned counterpart, Vicuna-13B (Chiang et al., 2023). We detail their implementation details in the next sections below. C.1 Open-source Models We implement multiple ICL approaches on LLaMA-13B and Vicuna-13B without fine-tuning. We set the maximum input length as 2048 and the batch size as 1. We run each experiment on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. To achieve this, we leverage the Accelerate  $^{13}$  framework and fp16 inference to save memory. We set maximum output length as 96 and sampling temperature as 0 (i.e., greedy decoding). We set both frequency_penalty and presence_penalty as 0. C.2 OpenAI Models We implement multiple ICL approaches on OpenAI models by calling their official APIs  $^{14}$ . We set the maximum input length as 3600 for all tasks and models. The only exception occurs when we use CODEX on RE tasks, where we set the maximum input length as 7000. We unify the maximum output length as 32 for RE task, and 96 for other three tasks. We set the sampling temperature coefficient as 0, i.e., greedy decoding. D Pivot Experiments on LLMs D.1 Sampling Temperature Existing prompt-engineering discussion<sup>15</sup> suggests setting the sampling temperature  $t = 0$  for tasks with structured outputs, including IE tasks. We validate this conclusion in Table 8, from which we could see the generated quality when  $t = 0$  is much higher than the quality when  $t \neq 0$ . Therefore we set  $t = 0$  in all main experiments, and do not take self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023c) into account. D.2 Automatic Chain-of-thought We additionally investigate whether rationales could facilitate LLMs' performance on few-shot IE tasks. Since there exists no golden rationales in original datasets, we follow Automatic Chain-of-thought (Auto-CoT; Zhang et al. 2023b) method as below. Regarding each sample, we query LLMs According to [sentence], Why [span] is a [label]. For example, given the sentence "DSC and Traction Control on all Speed3 models is also standard.", we would feed LLM the query that "Could you explain why Speed3 is a kind of car". Then we insert the bootstrapped rationales between the sentences and ground-truth answers. If a sentence has no positive labels, however, we do not ask LLMs and keep the original format as the vanilla ICL approach. Here we prompt InstructGPT to generate the rationales with temperature  $t = 0.7$ . We compare the performance with and without Auto-CoT as shown in Table 9. We are frustrated to find Auto-CoT degrades the performance with a large margin. We speculate this degradation could be attributed to three main reasons. (1) The rationale increase the length of each sample and thus decrease the overall example number in demos. (2) There exists an obvious discrepancy between sentences with and without positive labels. The rationales are only provided for sentences with positive labels because it is hard to explain why a sentence dose not contain any label. (3) Some auto-generated rationales are low-quality, especially for RE tasks. We would explore better strategy to exploit auto-genertaed rationales in the future work.

This page details experimental setups and results for few-shot information extraction tasks using large language models. It describes the implementation of both closed-source (OpenAI's CODEX, InstructGPT, ChatGPT) and open-source (LLaMA-13B, Vicuna-13B) models, specifying hyperparameters like input length, batch size, and sampling temperature. The main focus is on two pivot experiments: one validating that a sampling temperature of t=0 yields superior performance (Table 8), and another investigating Automatic Chain-of-thought (Auto-CoT), which surprisingly degrades performance across all tasks (Table 9). The text provides specific F1-scores and discusses potential reasons for the Auto-CoT failure.

**Text Evidence:**
- Experiments use OpenAI models (CODEX, InstructGPT, ChatGPT) via APIs and open-source models (LLaMA-13B, Vicuna-13B) without fine-tuning.
- For all main experiments, the sampling temperature is set to 0 (greedy decoding).
- Table 8 shows that setting t=0 produces significantly higher F1-scores than t=0.7 for all three datasets (FewNERD, TACREV, ACE05).
- Table 9 demonstrates that Auto-CoT drastically reduces performance, with F1-score drops of 17.4 points on FewNERD, 35.3 points on TACREV, and 4.6 points on ACE05.
- The authors speculate the degradation is due to increased sample length, label discrepancy, and low-quality generated rationales.

We run each experiment on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. To achieve this, we leverage the Accelerate  $^{13}$  framework and fp16 inference to save memory. We set maximum output length as 96 and sampling temperature as 0 (i.e., greedy decoding). We set both frequency_penalty and presence_penalty as 0. C.2 OpenAI Models We implement multiple ICL approaches on OpenAI models by calling their official APIs  $^{14}$ . We set the maximum input length as 3600 for all tasks and models. The only exception occurs when we use CODEX on RE tasks, where we set the maximum input length as 7000. We unify the maximum output length as 32 for RE task, and 96 for other three tasks. We set the sampling temperature coefficient as 0, i.e., greedy decoding. D Pivot Experiments on LLMs D.1 Sampling Temperature Existing prompt-engineering discussion<sup>15</sup> suggests setting the sampling temperature  $t = 0$  for tasks with structured outputs, including IE tasks. We validate this conclusion in Table 8, from which we could see the generated quality when  $t = 0$  is much higher than the quality when  $t \neq 0$ . Therefore we set  $t = 0$  in all main experiments, and do not take self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023c) into account. D.2 Automatic Chain-of-thought We additionally investigate whether rationales could facilitate LLMs' performance on few-shot IE tasks. Since there exists no golden rationales in original datasets, we follow Automatic Chain-of-thought (Auto-CoT; Zhang et al. 2023b) method as below. Regarding each sample, we query LLMs According to [sentence], Why [span] is a [label]. For example, given the sentence "DSC and Traction Control on all Speed3 models is also standard.", we would feed LLM the query that "Could you explain why Speed3 is a kind of car". Then we insert the bootstrapped rationales between the sentences and ground-truth answers. If a sentence has no positive labels, however, we do not ask LLMs and keep the original format as the vanilla ICL approach. Here we prompt InstructGPT to generate the rationales with temperature  $t = 0.7$ . We compare the performance with and without Auto-CoT as shown in Table 9. We are frustrated to find Auto-CoT degrades the performance with a large margin. We speculate this degradation could be attributed to three main reasons. (1) The rationale increase the length of each sample and thus decrease the overall example number in demos. (2) There exists an obvious discrepancy between sentences with and without positive labels. The rationales are only provided for sentences with positive labels because it is hard to explain why a sentence dose not contain any label. (3) Some auto-generated rationales are low-quality, especially for RE tasks. We would explore better strategy to exploit auto-genertaed rationales in the future work.

This page details experimental setups and results for few-shot information extraction tasks using large language models. It describes the implementation of both closed-source (OpenAI's CODEX, InstructGPT, ChatGPT) and open-source (LLaMA-13B, Vicuna-13B) models, specifying hyperparameters like input length, batch size, and sampling temperature. The main focus is on two pivot experiments: one validating that a sampling temperature of t=0 yields superior performance (Table 8), and another investigating Automatic Chain-of-thought (Auto-CoT), which surprisingly degrades performance across all tasks (Table 9). The text provides specific F1-scores and discusses potential reasons for the Auto-CoT failure.

**Text Evidence:**
- Experiments use OpenAI models (CODEX, InstructGPT, ChatGPT) via APIs and open-source models (LLaMA-13B, Vicuna-13B) without fine-tuning.
- For all main experiments, the sampling temperature is set to 0 (greedy decoding).
- Table 8 shows that setting t=0 produces significantly higher F1-scores than t=0.7 for all three datasets (FewNERD, TACREV, ACE05).
- Table 9 demonstrates that Auto-CoT drastically reduces performance, with F1-score drops of 17.4 points on FewNERD, 35.3 points on TACREV, and 4.6 points on ACE05.
- The authors speculate the degradation is due to increased sample length, label discrepancy, and low-quality generated rationales.

D.3 GPT-4 v.s. Others We tend to minimize the GPT-4 calls due to its high price. Thus we utilize 20-/100-shot settings across each dataset to compare GPT-4's performance with other LLMs. Table 10 reveals that GPT-4 does not outperform other LLMs significantly, except on OntoNotes and MAVEN. However, even on these datasets, GPT-4 still falls behind supervised SLMs by a significant margin. Consequently, the exclusion of GPT-4 does not undermine the conclusions drawn from our main experiments, and we omit it from our empirical study. E Auxiliary Experiments E.1 LLMs struggle on Fine-grained Datasets Based on the results shown in Figure 2, we additionally provide a quantitative analysis to show that LLMs struggle with fine-grained datasets. Under the 5-shot setting, we compare the performance difference of LLMs (ChatGPT) and SLMs (SoTA few-shot models) among different datasets. For each IE task, we observe a clear negative corre lation between the label number (row 2) and the performance difference (row 5). In other words, with more label types, LLMs tend to perform relatively worse than SLMs. Therefore we conclude that LLMs struggle on fine-grained datasets. E.2 Finding Better Instruction To investigate whether LLMs would benefit from complex instructions, we explored six instruction variants from simple to complex. Take NER task as an example, we illustrate them as below. Instruction0: [empty] Instruction1: Identify the entities expressed by each sentence, and locate each entity to words in the sentence. The possible entity types are: [Type_1], [Type_2], ..., [Type_N]. If you do not find any entity in this sentence, just output 'Answer: No entities found.' Instruction2: Identify the entities expressed by each sentence, and locate each entity to words in the sentence. This page presents a detailed analysis of large language models (LLMs) compared to supervised state-of-the-art (SoTA) models across various information extraction tasks. Section D.3 discusses the performance of GPT-4 relative to other LLMs like InstructGPT and CODEX, using Table 10 to show that GPT-4 does not significantly outperform others except on OntoNotes and MAVEN, and still lags behind supervised SLMs. Section E.1 provides a quantitative analysis from Table 11, demonstrating that LLMs struggle with fine-grained datasets, as evidenced by a negative correlation between the number of label types and performance difference. Section E.2 explores different instruction formats for the NER task, illustrating six variants from simple to complex.

**Text Evidence:**
- GPT-4 is excluded from the empirical study due to its high cost and lack of significant performance advantage over other LLMs.
- Table 10 shows GPT-4's F1-scores are competitive but not superior, with notable exceptions on OntoNotes (65.6) and MAVEN (52.1).
- Table 11 quantifies the performance gap between LLMs (ChatGPT) and SLMs, showing LLMs perform worse on datasets with more labels (e.g., -3.9 ΔF1 on FewNERD with 66 entity types).
- The text concludes that LLMs struggle on fine-grained datasets due to the negative correlation between label count and performance difference.
- Six instruction variants are explored for the NER task, ranging from an empty prompt (Instruction0) to complex instructions involving definitions and specific formatting (Instruction3).

Even the prompt without instruction (I0) leads to comparable, if not better, results than prompt with complex instructions. Therefore, we use simple instruction (I1) in our main experiment. E.3 Do More Samples in Demos Help? We wonder whether longer demos bring more powerful ICL abilities for LLMs. Thus we investigate the impact of increasing the number of demonstrations on LLMs' performance in Figure 8. We observe that: (1) The performance of the RE task consistently improves with more demos, indicating its potential benefiting from additional annotations. (2) The NER and ED tasks reach a stable or degraded performance with increased demo numbers, suggesting that they are limited even before reaching the maximum input length. (3) Open-source LLMs, i.e., LLaMA and Vicuna, have more limited capacities in leveraging demos compared to OpenAI models, with their performance stagnating or even collapsing with only a few (2-4) demos. E.4 Finding Better Demo Selection Strategy The maximum input length of LLMs usually limits the sentence number in demos even under few-shot settings. For each test sentence  $s$ , we demand a demo retriever  $\mathcal{E}(D,s)$  which selects a subset from  $D$  as the sentences in demo. Following previous work, we consider three commonly-used strategies. (1) Random sampling. (2) Sentence-embedding (Liu et al., 2022; Su et al., 2022): retrieving the top-K nearest sentences measured by sentence embedding. We compute the embeddings by SimCSE-RoBERTa-large (Gao et al., 2021). (3) Efficient Prompt Retriever (Rubin et al., 2022): retrieving by a neural retriever  $R$  trained on  $D$ .

For each test sentence  $s$ , we pre-retrieve  $M$  similar sentences  $\bar{D} = \{(s_i', y_i')\}_{i=1}^M \subset D$ . Then we score each sentence in  $\bar{D}$  by their likelihoods  $P_{\mathcal{L}}(f(y_i') | f(s_i'))$  where  $f$  denotes the prompt format adopted and  $\mathcal{L}$  the scoring LM. This page discusses the limitations of Large Language Models (LLMs) in handling easy samples, attributing their poor performance to false-positive predictions for negative samples. It identifies two primary causes: LLM hallucination and span boundary mismatch. The section provides two detailed case studies illustrating these issues: Case 1 shows an LLM incorrectly identifying "die" as a person entity, while Case 2 demonstrates it misclassifying the preposition "of" as an organization. The text explains that LLMs often generate meaningless or confusing outputs due to a lack of specific fine-tuning on Information Extraction (IE) tasks.

**Text Evidence:**
- LLMs make two kinds of erroneous predictions: lack of external knowledge and limited reasoning abilities.
- The inferior performance on easy samples is attributed to false-positive predictions for negative samples.
- Two main reasons for incorrect cases are LLM hallucination and span boundary mismatch.
- Case 1: LLMs predict "die" as an entity person-other when the ground truth is None.
- Case 2: LLMs predict "of" as an entity organization-other when the ground truth is None.
- LLMs sometimes hallucinate and provide meaningless explanations or answers without specific fine-tuning on IE tasks.

This page discusses the limitations of sample-level approaches in large language models (LLMs) for named entity recognition (NER) and entity disambiguation (ED), highlighting the span boundary mismatching problem. This page discusses the limitations of sample-level approaches in large language models (LLMs) for named entity recognition (NER) and entity disambiguation (ED), highlighting the span boundary mismatching problem. It presents two case studies: Case 3 shows an LLM incorrectly classifying "Baron" as a person, while Case 4 shows it misclassifying "65th" as an award. The page also introduces the "adaptive filter-then-rerank paradigm," which converts few-shot information extraction tasks into multiple-choice questions, with demonstration examples provided for the FewNERD, TACREV, and ACE05 datasets in Tables 16, 17, and 18 respectively, and templates listed in Tables 19, 20, and 21.

**Text Evidence:**
- Sample-level approaches in LLMs consider each word/span candidate independently, leading to span boundary mismatching.
- Easy samples suffer more from boundary mismatching than hard samples.
- In Case 3, LLMs predict "Baron" (a subspan of "Baron Carl Hurleman") as "person-other" when the ground-truth is "None".
- In Case 4, LLMs predict "65th" (a subspan of "65th British Academy Film Awards") as "other-awards" when the ground-truth is "None".
- The adaptive filter-then-rerank paradigm converts few-shot IE tasks to multiple-choice questions.
- Demonstration examples are shown in Table 16 (FewNERD), Table 17 (TACREV), and Table 18 (ACE05).

| Personnel.Elect | The word {evt} triggers an ELECT event which implies an election.
| Personnel.Start-Position | The word {evt} triggers a START-POSITION event: a PERSON elected or appointed begins working for (or changes offices within) an ORGANIZATION or GOVERNMENT.
| Personnel.Nominate | The word {evt} triggers a NOMINATE event: a PERSON is proposed for a position through official channels.
| Conflict.Attack | The word {evt} triggers an ATTACK event: a violent physical act causing harm or damage.
| Personnel.End-Position | The word {evt} triggers an END-POSITION event: a PERSON stops working for (or changes offices within) an ORGANIZATION or GOVERNMENT.
| Contact.Meet | The word {evt} triggers a MEET event: two or more entities come together at a single location and interact with one another face-to-face.
| Life.Marry | The word {evt} triggers a MARRY event: two people are married under the legal definition.
| Contact.Phone-Write | The word {evt} triggers a PHONE-WRITE event: two or more people directly engage in discussion which does not take place 'face-to-face'.
| Transaction.Transform-Money | The word {evt} triggers a TRANSFER-MONEY event: giving, receiving, borrowing, or lending money when it is NOT in the context of purchasing something.
| Justice.Sue | The word {evt} triggers a SUE event: a court proceeding has been initiated for the purposes of determining the liability of a PERSON, ORGANIZATION or GEOPOLITICAL ENTITY accused of committing a crime or neglecting a commitment
| Conflict.Demonstrate | The word {evt} triggers a DEMONSTRATE event: a large number of people come together in a public area to protest or demand some sort of official action. For example: protests, sit-ins, strikes and riots.
| Business.End-Org | The word {evt} triggers an END-ORG event: an ORGANIZATION ceases to exist (in other words, goes out of business).
| Life.Injure | The word {evt} triggers an INJURE event: a PERSON gets/got injured whether it occurs accidentally, intentionally or even self-inflicted.
| Life.Die | The word {evt} triggers a DIE event: a PERSON dies/died whether it occurs accidentally, intentionally or even self-inflicted.
| Justice.Arrest-Jail | The word {evt} triggers a ARREST-JAIL event: a PERSON is sent to prison.
| Transaction.Transfer-Ownership | The word {evt} triggers a TRANSFER-OWNERSHIP event: The buying, selling, loaning, borrowing, giving, or receiving of artifacts or organizations by an individual or organization.
| Justice.Execute | The word {evt} triggers an EXECUTE event: a PERSON is/was executed
| Justice.Trial-Hearing | The word {evt} triggers a TRIAL-HEARING event: a court proceeding has been initiated for the purposes of determining the guilt or innocence of a PERSON, ORGANIZATION or GEOPOLITICAL ENTITY accused of committing a crime.
| Justice.Sentence | The word {evt} triggers a SENTENCE event: the punishment for the DEFENDANT is issued
